entry.lemma: šôp̄ār 'ram's horn (as a signal instrument)'; yôḇēl 'ram' (later 'jubilee'); qeren 'horn'
entry.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine (pl. šôp̄rôṯ / šôp̄ārôṯ); construct phrases
entry.literal: ram's horn; horns of the rams; the horn of the ram
entry.standardEnglish: trumpet (ASV, KJV, NRSV); horn (NJPS); trumpets of rams' horns (ASV Josh 6:4)
entry.wohChoice: 'shofar' (transliterated; plural 'shofars') for šôp̄ār in every context: Sinai ('the sound of a shofar', Ex 19:16, 19; 20:18 in the exodus-woh numbering); the Jericho rite ('seven shofars of rams' horns', Josh 6:4, 6, 8, 13; 'the sound of the shofar', 6:5, 20; 'blow the shofars', 6:4, 8, 9, 13, 16, 20); mustering ('he blew the shofar', Judg 6:34); royal acclamation ('blow the shofar', 1 Kgs 1:34, 39, 41). 'ram's horn' / 'rams' horns' for yôḇēl and qeren hayyôḇēl (Josh 6:4-8, 13; exodus-woh Ex 19:13). 'trumpet' is reserved for the metal ḥăṣōṣərâ (Num 10:2-10; 2 Kgs 11:14).
entry.rationale: **Promotion to central.** The decision was first made in two overlays, exodus-woh at Sinai (overlay sinai-cloud-fire-thunder-trumpet-imagery-exodus-compositional-cluster-overlay, with yobel-rams-horn-jubilee-horn-translation-convention-exodus-19-13-overlay for yôḇēl) and 1-kings-woh at Shelomoh's accession (shofar-coronation-signal-1-kings-1, whose rationale names a third book as the trigger for promotion). Joshua 6 and Judges 6 are the third and fourth books, so the decision moves here; the Kings overlay entry should be retired in favour of this id (or kept as a pointer) when the diff is applied, and the exodus-woh overlay entries may cite it. // **The instrument.** The šôp̄ār is the horn of a ram (or other animal) used as a signal instrument; it produces a few natural tones and serves for alarm, assembly, war, cultic proclamation and royal acclamation (Braun, Music in Ancient Israel/Palestine, 2002; Jones, 'Music and Musical Instruments', ABD IV, 1992; BDB; HALOT). The Hebrew Bible distinguishes it from the ḥăṣōṣərâ, the straight metal trumpet made of hammered silver (Num 10:2), and both appear side by side (Ps 98:6; 1 Chr 15:28; 2 Chr 15:14). English 'trumpet' (ASV, KJV, NRSV) translates both and so merges two instruments the Hebrew keeps apart, while 'horn' (NJPS) is accurate but generic (qeren 'horn' is a separate word, used in Josh 6:5). 'shofar' is a standard English loanword, current through its continued Jewish liturgical use, and is used in every context so that one Hebrew word has one English form. // **yôḇēl.** In Josh 6:4-13 and Ex 19:13 yôḇēl is the ram (BDB yôḇēl 1, cf. Phoenician ybl 'ram'), and the instrument is the ram's horn; the later sense 'jubilee' (Lev 25:10-13) derives from the horn that announced the year. šôp̄rôṯ hayyôḇəlîm is rendered 'shofars of rams' horns' and qeren hayyôḇēl 'the ram's horn'. // **Reception.** The English and French Bibles quoted in The Book Which Tells the Truth (ch. 3) have 'trumpet' at Josh 6:5, and the canon reads the Jericho instrument as a complex sound device. The transliteration is chosen for the lexical reason given above, not to make or avoid that reading; the reading is confined to labelled reception notes. The entry is direct: it renders the Hebrew noun by its established loanword and records the instrument's identity, which is not disputed. // **Application note.** The Exodus sites are taken from the 1-kings-woh entry (EXO-WOH-19:16, 19; 20:18); the orchestrator should check them against the exodus-woh refIds (MT 20:15 = ET 20:18) and the parallel Exodus Editor pass.

entry.translit: ʾărôn ; ʾărôn habbərîṯ ; ʾărôn YHWH ; ʾărôn hāʾĕlōhîm ; ʾărôn ʾĕlōhê yiśrāʾēl
entry.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine (usually with the article or in construct)
entry.literal: the chest; the chest of the covenant / of YHWH / of the God / of the God of Israel
entry.standardEnglish: the ark; the ark of the covenant; the ark of Jehovah; the ark of God; the ark of the God of Israel (ASV)
entry.wohChoice: 'the ark' for the cultic ʾărôn, with its genitive rendered as the Hebrew gives it at each site: 'the ark of the covenant (of YHWH)' (Josh 6:6, 8), 'the ark of YHWH' (Josh 6:6, 7, 11-13; 1 Sam 5:3, 4; 6:1-21 passim), 'the ark of the Elohim' (articular; 1 Sam 5:1, 2, 10, 11), 'the ark of Elohim' (anarthrous; 1 Sam 3:3), 'the ark of the Elohim of Yisra'el' (in Pelishti speech; 1 Sam 5:7, 8, 10, 11; 6:3); the bare noun 'the ark' (Josh 6:4, 9, 13; 1 Sam 6:13, 15). Non-cultic ʾărôn is 'coffin' (Gen 50:26) or 'chest' (2 Kgs 12:10-11).
entry.rationale: ʾărôn is an ordinary word for a box or chest (Gen 50:26 Yosef's coffin; 2 Kgs 12:10-11 the collection chest), and its cultic referent is the wooden chest overlaid with gold, carried on poles, that held the tablets of the covenant (Ex 25:10-22; Deut 10:1-5; 1 Kgs 8:9) and was associated with YHWH's presence enthroned above the cherubim (1 Sam 4:4; 2 Sam 6:2) (Seow, 'Ark of the Covenant', ABD I, 1992; de Vaux, Ancient Israel, 1961; Haran, Temples and Temple-Service in Ancient Israel, 1978). 'Ark' (Latin arca 'chest') is the established English term and is kept. The Hebrew uses several genitives, which modern scholarship connects with different traditions about the object, the Deuteronomistic 'ark of the covenant' (a container of the tablets) and the older 'ark of YHWH / of the Elohim' (the war palladium and throne of the ark narrative, 1 Sam 4-6; 2 Sam 6) (Miller and Roberts, The Hand of the Lord, 1977; Campbell, The Ark Narrative, 1975); the translation renders each genitive as it stands, including the article on ʾĕlōhîm under the elohim-referent conventions, and does not harmonize them. In the ark narrative the ark is the locus of YHWH's power against the Pelishtim and against Israelites who treat it improperly (1 Sam 5:1-12; 6:19; 2 Sam 6:6-7), which the commentary describes in the terms of the text. The Book Which Tells the Truth (ch. 3) reads the ark as housing a transmitter-receiver with its own power source; that reading is confined to labelled reception notes, and the line uses no technical vocabulary. The entry is direct. **Coordination note:** if the parallel Exodus Editor pass creates an entry for ʾărôn at Ex 25, the two should be merged under one id, with these sites in its appliesTo.

entry.lemma: dāḡôn, the Philistine name of the West-Semitic deity Dagan
entry.wohChoice: 'Dagon' (the Hebrew form, identical in English) in Hebrew-Bible sources: 1 Sam 5:2-5, 7; also Judg 16:23 and 1 Chr 10:10 when translated. The Ugaritic form Daganu is governed by the sibling entry dagan-dagon-grain-deity-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bible-philistine-pantheon.
entry.rationale: The Ugaritic central entry dagan-dagon-grain-deity-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bible-philistine-pantheon asks that 'a future Hebrew Editor pass on Judg 16:23 or 1 Sam 5' produce the Hebrew central entry on the Philistine Dagon, with a bidirectional back-reference; this is that entry. Dagan is a West-Semitic god attested from the third millennium at Ebla and Mari, worshipped at Ugarit (where Baʿlu is called 'son of Dagan') and in Iron-Age Philistia, whose name is generally connected with *dgn* 'grain' (Hebrew dāḡān) (Healey, 'Dagon', DDD, 2nd ed., 1999; Singer, 'Towards the Image of Dagon the God of the Philistines', Syria 69, 1992; Day, Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan, 2000); the Philistines adopted the local deity, which the Hebrew Bible presents as their national god (Judg 16:23; 1 Sam 5:2-7; 1 Chr 10:10). The Hebrew form dāḡôn is used, unchanged in English, as the ASV and all versions do. The derivation from dāḡ 'fish' and the image of a fish-tailed god are later folk etymology, partly built on the MT of 1 Sam 5:4 (raq dāḡôn nišʾar ʿālāyw 'only Dagon was left to him'), which the commentary there discusses; the Hebrew does not describe the image's form. 1 Sam 5 narrates the image falling prostrate before the ark and then broken, a polemic of YHWH's superiority in the god's own house (McCarter, I Samuel, AB 8, 1980; Miller and Roberts, The Hand of the Lord, 1977). The canon's reading of the scene (The Book Which Tells the Truth, ch. 3: an electrical discharge from the ark) is confined to a labelled reception note. The entry is direct.

changes.rationale:
**The Northwest-Semitic grain-deity.** Ugaritic *Daganu* (alphabetic-cuneiform *dgn*) is attested as **Baʿlu's father** — the standing epithet *bn dgn* 'Son of Daganu' is applied to Baʿlu throughout KTU 1.2 (1.2-i:18, 35, 38, 40). The paternity-relation is fixed across the Ugaritic mythological corpus, although Daganu himself appears only rarely as a narrative-figure (the Baal Cycle has Baʿlu interacting with ʾIlu, his grandfather-figure-by-marriage, rather than with Daganu directly). The lexeme *dgn* has two main etymological proposals: (i) cereal-grain (cognate to Phoenician and Aramaic *dāgān* 'grain'); (ii) rain-cloud (Healey's less-common alternative). The grain-deity reading is the consensus.

**Cross-corpus attestation across the Levant and Mesopotamia.**
- **Mari (Old Babylonian)** — *Dagan* is one of the principal deities of the Mari pantheon (18th c. BCE). Attestation in royal-inscription and personal-name material.
- **Emar (Late Bronze Age)** — *Dagan* is a major cult-figure at Emar (on the Middle Euphrates); the Emar ritual-texts give extensive evidence of his cult.
- **Ugarit (Late Bronze Age)** — attested as Baʿlu's father; smaller cult-presence than the Mari/Emar evidence would suggest, indicating a regionally-diffused divine figure with shifting prominence.
- **The Philistine pantheon (Iron Age I-II)** — *Dāgôn* is the principal deity of Ashdod, Gaza, and Ashkelon. The Philistine adoption of Daganu is widely interpreted (Singer 1992; Day 2000) as the Aegean-migrant Philistines absorbing the local West-Semitic divine name into their adapted pantheon.

**Cross-corpus Hebrew Bible — the Philistine Dagon.** Hebrew Bible attestations of *Dāgôn*:
- **Judg 16:23-30** — Samson destroys the temple of Dagon at Gaza; *va-yiqr'u et Dagon eloheihem* 'they called Dagon their god'.
- **1 Sam 5:1-7** — the ark-narrative; the captured Israelite ark is placed in the temple of Dagon at Ashdod; Dagon's image falls before the ark twice and is finally broken (*ve-rosh Dagon u-shtei kappot yadav k'rutot* 'the head of Dagon and his two hand-palms were cut off').
- **1 Chr 10:10** — Saul's head placed in Dagon's temple by the Philistines.

The Hebrew Bible's Dagon-polemic is thus specifically **anti-Philistine cult-polemic**, distinct from the broader anti-Canaanite Baʿal-and-Asherah polemic. The Iron Age I Philistine takeover of the West-Semitic Daganu cult and the Hebrew-Israelite contest with the Philistines are the historical context.

**Cross-corpus Mesopotamian and the Akkadian-side.** Akkadian *Dagan* is attested at Mari, in personal-names across the Old Babylonian and Late Babylonian periods, and in royal-inscriptional material. The Mari evidence is particularly rich — letters and rituals from the royal archive of Zimri-Lim. **Itamar Singer**, *Hittite and Northern Hittite Studies presented to Hans G. Güterbock on the Occasion of his 75th Birthday* (1992) — important treatment. **A. Archi**, 'Cult of the Ancestors and Tutelary God at Ebla,' in *Fucus: A Semitic/Afrasian Gathering in Remembrance of Albert Ehrman* (Amsterdam 1988) on the Eblaite background.

**Named-scholarship frame.** **J. F. Healey**, 'Dagon,' in K. van der Toorn et al. (eds.), *Dictionary of Deities and Demons in the Bible* (2nd ed., Leiden 1999), pp. 216-219. **I. Singer**, *Hittite Studies* (1992) — see above. **J. Day**, *Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan* (JSOTSup 265, Sheffield 2000), pp. 85-90 on Dagon. **B. Doak**, *The Last of the Rephaim: Conquest and Cataclysm in the Heroic Ages of Ancient Israel* (Boston 2012) on the Philistine context. **L. E. Stager**, 'Forging an Identity: The Emergence of Ancient Israel,' in *The Oxford History of the Biblical World* (Oxford 1998) on the broader Iron Age I Philistine cult-context.

**Bidirectional cross-references.** Cluster with new Ugaritic central entries `baal-ugaritic-baalu-storm-god-cross-corpus-hebrew-bible-polemic` (Baʿlu's parentage), `el-ugaritic-ilu-northwest-semitic-pantheon-head-cross-corpus`. Future Hebrew Editor pass on Judg 16:23 or 1 Sam 5 should produce the Hebrew central entry on the Philistine Dagon-polemic with bidirectional back-reference.

**Lens-discipline operational disavowals.** (i) **No Sitchin-corpus reading of Daganu as Anunnaki-fish-deity** (a popular fringe-reading conflating Daganu with Akkadian *Oannes / Adapa* via the false-etymological *dag* 'fish' Hebrew). Daganu is the **grain-deity** (proto-Semitic *√dgn* 'grain'); the *dag* 'fish' Hebrew folk-etymology, popularized in 19th c. comparative-religion literature and resurrected in Sitchin-corpus material, is **philologically incorrect**. The fish-iconography sometimes associated with Dagon in popular literature derives from a misreading of 1 Sam 5:4 *raq Dagon nišʾar ʿalav* '(only Dagon's stump remained on him') as a fish-tail reference; the Hebrew text does not support this. (ii) **No syncretistic Christian-typology** mapping Daganu/Dagon onto later traditions.

**Back-reference (v2.84.0).** The Hebrew-Bible sibling requested above now exists: `dagon-philistine-deity-hebrew-bible-cross-corpus` governs the Hebrew form 'Dagon' (1 Sam 5:2-7; Judg 16:23; 1 Chr 10:10), with a back-reference to this entry.
